Price before you optimize — and the price list corrected the easy story twice. The 12-session pilot said input bulk beats all tool results and that big results are rare; the full-fleet census flipped both: tool RESULTS are 71.8% of context-entering bytes, and results ≥10KB hold 68.1% of those bytes. The epic's biggest wins are the un-briefed manifest, a deterministic tabular render tier, and cards complete enough to avoid the follow-up call.

The pilot (12 sessions) found tool_use INPUT bulk larger than all tool results, and my emerging shape ranked an input-side discipline as wave 1. blocks.title: Pilot correction #1 — the direction flip

content.value: The pilot's flat-distribution claim (results ≥10KB = 14.6% of bytes) does not hold at fleet scale: ≥10KB results hold 68.1% of result bytes, ≥50KB hold 44.8%. blocks.text: Determinism and cache economics — why early bytes cost 5–6x

content.value: The meter: cache writes at 2x rate_in (1h TTL), cache reads at 0.1x per remaining turn, output at 5x rate_in. A byte entering context early in a long session is written once and re-read every turn — the manifest consumed at session start is amplified roughly 5–6x its nominal size. That is why the un-briefed manifest outranks payloads that are nominally larger but arrive late.

blocks.text: Risks and unknowns

items.value: Byte-to-token fidelity: TSV's 1.7–5.5x byte wins are unproven in tokens. Likely to grow (JSON punctuation tokenizes badly), but METER.md's 30% cross-model divergence means no number ships until count_tokens runs. If no key ever materializes, publish byte figures with an explicit conversion-pending label.

Briefing may cost correctness: TSV drops self-describing keys, and agents script against exactly the claim-protocol fields. The duel is the only honest answer; it gates the serialization wave, and its budget (~$30–80) is a user ratification call.

Sample sensitivity: bp share moves 5.37% → 7.66% on one excluded project; the pilot-vs-fleet reversals prove small samples mislead here. The pre/post-AXI comparison (9.4% → 4.7%) is confounded by workload drift — a within-session-type cut is future work.

Several 12-session pilot facts carry no rerun command (DEMOTED-NO-RERUN): the 4.7% share, the flat distribution, the 428-vs-56 climb ratio, the original TSV pilot renders. Where a storm probe re-measured with a saved script (fleet census, field census, fixtures), the storm number is canonical; pilot-only numbers are agent-memory grade.

Near-dead fields: updated_at (491 refs) is a real cut candidate; the criteria pair is too new to judge. Cut-with-escape-hatch, never proof-before-cut — and any card change re-freezes the byte tripwires in the same PR.
Input-side bulk (473 MB fleet-wide) now has a measured size but no owner: recommendation is a doctrine line (write scripts as files, reference by path), not a wave. Explicitly a user scope call.
MCP wave sequencing: with 4 calls of history, shipping resource_link before deliberate exercise sessions would build on zero evidence. Exercise first, then decide.

Cross-lane dependency: whether rev rides on the brief card is ruled in the view-tiers and handle-doctrine papers; this lane's usage data (rev = 7,920 refs) supports carriage but does not decide the mechanism (card field vs board profile vs events-only invalidation).

This is the spend-census lane Paper of the Barkpark context-compression program: the internal evidence the epic charter will rank its waves by. The thesis Price before you optimize — and the price list corrected the easy story twice. The 12-session pilot said input bulk beats all tool results and that big results are rare; the full-fleet census flipped both: tool RESULTS are 71.8% of context-entering bytes, and results ≥10KB hold 68.1% of those bytes. What survived both scales: bp's own outputs are a single-digit share (5.37%), Read and foreign tools dominate, and under 58.8%-cache-write economics the cost driver is TURNS, not payload spikes. The meter: cache writes at 2x rate_in (1h TTL), cache reads at 0.1x per remaining turn, output at 5x rate_in.   • Briefing may cost correctness: TSV drops self-describing keys, and agents script against exactly the claim-protocol fields. The duel is the only honest answer; it gates the serialization wave, and its budget (~$30–80) is a user ratification call.
  • Sample sensitivity: bp share moves 5.37% → 7.66% on one excluded project; the pilot-vs-fleet reversals prove small samples mislead here. The pre/post-AXI comparison (9.4% → 4.7%) is confounded by workload drift — a within-session-type cut is future work.
  • Several 12-session pilot facts carry no rerun command (DEMOTED-NO-RERUN): the 4.7% share, the flat distribution, the 428-vs-56 climb ratio, the original TSV pilot renders. Where a storm probe re-measured with a saved script (fleet census, field census, fixtures), the storm number is canonical; pilot-only numbers are agent-memory grade.
  • Near-dead fields: updated_at (491 refs) is a real cut candidate; the criteria pair is too new to judge. Cut-with-escape-hatch, never proof-before-cut — and any card change re-freezes the byte tripwires in the same PR.
  • Input-side bulk (473 MB fleet-wide) now has a measured size but no owner: recommendation is a doctrine line (write scripts as files, reference by path), not a wave. Explicitly a user scope call.
  • MCP wave sequencing: with 4 calls of history, shipping resource_link before deliberate exercise sessions would build on zero evidence. Exercise first, then decide.
  • Cross-lane dependency: whether rev rides on the brief card is ruled in the view-tiers and handle-doctrine papers; this lane's usage data (rev = 7,920 refs) supports carriage but does not decide the mechanism (card field vs board profile vs events-only invalidation).
